patient.name: Desmond Clarke
patient.complaint: Central chest tightness at rest for 40 minutes, not eased by his GTN spray
background: Inferior MI with a stent in 2019

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with rest or crescendo chest pain, ST depression or T-wave inversion (or a normal ECG) and a **normal troponin**: the troponin separates unstable angina from NSTEMI.

points: Desmond, 64, known IHD with a stent from 2019.
Two weeks: angina on **less and less exertion**.
Tonight: central tightness **at rest** for 40 minutes.
Two puffs of GTN barely touched it.

steps.lead: Desmond's pain is new at rest after a **crescendo** fortnight: a plaque that has ruptured with **partial** thrombus, not yet killing muscle.
His **previous MI and stent** are the strongest pointer; his diabetes, hypertension and smoking history add to it.

points: Pain spreads to his **left arm and jaw**.
Chest clear, no murmur, no oedema.
Pain is not pleuritic and not positional.

steps.lead: Rest pain, radiation, sweating and nausea fit ACS. Only the **troponin** will tell us which type.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG at 8 minutes
visual.caption: Horizontal **ST depression** V3 to V6 with T-wave inversion in I and aVL. No ST elevation, so not a STEMI.

steps.text: Desmond's ECG within 10 minutes: ischaemia, but no ST elevation.

steps.q: Desmond has ST depression and his troponin comes back normal twice. What is this?
steps.r: Rest pain with ischaemic ECG changes but **no troponin rise** = unstable angina. A rise would make it NSTEMI.

steps.text: A normal ECG does **not** exclude unstable angina. The history makes the diagnosis; ECG and troponin sort the type.
Unstable angina is the only ACS with a **normal troponin**. If the stem gives a raised troponin, it is not unstable angina.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (12-lead ECG within 10 minutes) and questions on serial troponin and the GRACE score.

steps.q: Desmond arrives in triage with rest chest pain. What comes first?
steps.r: An **ECG within 10 minutes** of arrival sorts STEMI (cath lab now) from the rest. An exercise test is unsafe in suspected ACS.

steps.lead: Desmond gets his **ECG at 8 minutes**. CT coronary angiography is the first-line test for **stable** chest pain, not for an acute rest-pain presentation.

steps.text: Normal Hb and kidneys matter before antithrombotics and angiography.

visual.title: High-sensitivity troponin T
visual.caption: Both values sit **below the 99th centile** and do not rise: no necrosis, so unstable angina, not NSTEMI.

steps.lead: Clinical picture plus ECG plus a **flat, normal troponin** confirms Desmond has unstable angina rather than an NSTEMI.

steps.title: Chest pain at rest: the sorting pathway
nodes: No ST elevation → serial high-sensitivity troponin
steps.caption: The ECG and troponin are sorting tools; the history raised the alarm.

visual.title: GRACE score (6-month mortality risk)
visual.label: Desmond 132
visual.caption: Age, heart rate, ST depression and prior MI push Desmond into the **high-risk** band: early angiography.

steps.lead: Desmond's **GRACE score of 132** is high, so he is for early angiography rather than conservative care.

steps.text: Do not send a rest-pain patient for an **exercise tolerance test** or CTCA first. Those are for stable symptoms.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (aspirin 300 mg plus a second antiplatelet and fondaparinux) and 'next step' questions driven by GRACE risk, plus driving advice.

steps.q: Desmond's saturations are 97% on air. Which does he NOT need?
steps.r: Oxygen only if **SpO2 below 94%**. Routine oxygen in a non-hypoxic patient gives no benefit.

steps.lead: Desmond gets **aspirin 300 mg** plus **ticagrelor**, **fondaparinux**, GTN and morphine for pain, and no oxygen at 97%.
His GRACE is high, so Desmond goes for **coronary angiography plus PCI within 24 to 72 hours** rather than conservative care.

visual.title: Angiogram: culprit lesion
visual.caption: A ruptured plaque in the proximal **LAD** with non-occlusive thrombus; flow is reduced but preserved.

steps.text: Desmond's angiogram the next morning; a stent restores full flow.

steps.lead: Without treatment, Desmond's partial thrombus could **occlude** fully: MI, arrhythmia, heart failure or shock.
On discharge: lifelong aspirin, ticagrelor for **12 months**, high-intensity statin, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor.

steps.q: Desmond drives lorries for a living. What do you tell him?
o: Inform DVLA and stop driving until assessed
steps.r: He holds a **Group 2** licence, which has stricter standards. He must inform the DVLA and stop driving until assessed.

steps.lead: Desmond's care follows **NICE NG185**, with the **GRACE** score steering timing and **DVLA** standards for his job.

steps.text: Thrombolysis is for STEMI when PCI is not available in time. It has **no role** in unstable angina or NSTEMI.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the mechanism of unstable angina (plaque rupture with partial thrombus), why troponin stays normal, and how antiplatelets and fondaparinux act.

steps.lead: Desmond's LAD plaque **ruptured**, platelets piled on and a **partial** thrombus narrowed the lumen without blocking it.

steps.title: From plaque to unstable angina
nodes: Lipid-rich plaque with thin fibrous cap

steps.lead: Desmond's flow drop was **too small or too brief** to kill myocytes, so no troponin leaked out.

steps.q: Why did Desmond's troponin stay normal?
o: Ischaemia did not cause myocyte necrosis
The thrombus fully occluded the artery
Troponin is cleared by the kidneys
steps.r: Troponin is released when myocytes **die**. No necrosis, no troponin: that is the definition of unstable angina.

steps.lead: Desmond's unstable plaque could **propagate** thrombus to full occlusion at any time: high short-term MI risk.
Aspirin and ticagrelor block **platelets**; fondaparinux blocks **factor Xa** in the clotting cascade: two pathways, one thrombus.

steps.text: The exam likes **'partial thrombus, no necrosis'** for unstable angina versus **'complete occlusion'** for STEMI.

mcq.q: What blood result separates unstable angina from NSTEMI?
mcq.r: Unstable angina has a **normal troponin**; NSTEMI has a raised one.

mcq.q: What is the main risk factor for unstable angina in the notes?
mcq.r: **Previous IHD** is the main risk factor.

mcq.q: Which pain pattern fits unstable angina?
o: Pain only on exertion, eased by rest
Pain at rest or crescendo, not eased by GTN
mcq.r: Rest, new-onset or **crescendo** pain is unstable; exertional pain eased by rest is stable.

mcq.q: How quickly should the ECG be done in suspected ACS?
mcq.r: An ECG **within 10 minutes** of arrival picks out STEMI.

mcq.q: Which score guides early invasive versus conservative management?
What is the first-line anticoagulant in unstable angina?
When is oxygen given in unstable angina?
How long is the second antiplatelet continued after unstable angina?
mcq.r: Aspirin lifelong; second antiplatelet for **12 months**.

mcq.q: Which describes the thrombus in unstable angina?
mcq.r: Plaque rupture with **partial** thrombus; complete occlusion is STEMI.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Rest and crescendo pain with ST depression but a normal, unchanged troponin is unstable angina. A troponin rise would make it NSTEMI.

glossary.ACS: Acute coronary syndrome: unstable angina, NSTEMI or STEMI, all from a sudden coronary plaque event.
glossary.unstable angina: Ischaemic chest pain at rest or crescendo, with a normal troponin: ischaemia without necrosis.
glossary.stable angina: Predictable chest pain on exertion, eased by rest or GTN, from a fixed coronary narrowing.
glossary.NSTEMI: Non-ST elevation myocardial infarction: ACS with a raised troponin but no ST elevation.
glossary.STEMI: ST elevation myocardial infarction: complete coronary occlusion causing full-thickness infarction.
glossary.crescendo: Angina that becomes more frequent, longer or triggered by less effort over days to weeks.
glossary.troponin: Cardiac muscle protein released when myocytes die; raised in MI, normal in unstable angina.
glossary.99th centile: The upper reference limit for troponin; values above it indicate myocardial injury.
glossary.plaque rupture: Tearing of an atheroma's fibrous cap, exposing clot-promoting material to blood.
glossary.thrombus: A blood clot formed inside a vessel.
glossary.necrosis: Death of cells; in the heart it releases troponin.
glossary.ST depression: Downward shift of the ST segment on ECG, a sign of subendocardial ischaemia.
glossary.T-wave inversion: Upside-down T waves on ECG, which can indicate ischaemia.
glossary.LBBB: Left bundle branch block; when new with chest pain it is treated like STEMI.
glossary.GRACE score: Risk score in ACS predicting mortality, used to choose early angiography or conservative care.
glossary.GTN: Glyceryl trinitrate: a nitrate spray or tablet that dilates veins and coronary arteries to ease angina.
glossary.DAPT: Dual antiplatelet therapy: aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor such as clopidogrel or ticagrelor.
glossary.P2Y12: Platelet ADP receptor blocked by clopidogrel and ticagrelor to reduce platelet aggregation.
glossary.clopidogrel: P2Y12 inhibitor antiplatelet given with aspirin in ACS.
glossary.ticagrelor: Reversible P2Y12 inhibitor antiplatelet given with aspirin in ACS.
glossary.fondaparinux: Subcutaneous factor Xa inhibitor; first-line anticoagulant in unstable angina and NSTEMI.
glossary.LMWH: Low molecular weight heparin, e.g. enoxaparin; an injectable anticoagulant.
glossary.factor Xa: Clotting factor that converts prothrombin to thrombin; target of fondaparinux.
glossary.PCI: Percutaneous coronary intervention: balloon and stent via a catheter to open a coronary artery.
glossary.coronary angiography: Catheter test injecting dye into the coronary arteries to show narrowing or clot.
glossary.CT coronary angiography: CT scan with contrast showing coronary arteries; first-line test for stable chest pain.
glossary.secondary prevention: Treatment after an event to stop another: antiplatelets, statin, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor.
glossary.high-intensity statin: Statin at a dose that cuts LDL by over 40%, e.g. atorvastatin 80 mg.
glossary.DVLA: The UK licensing agency that patients must inform about conditions affecting driving.
glossary.Group 2: Vocational driving licence (lorries and buses) with stricter medical standards.
glossary.cardiogenic shock: Low blood pressure and poor perfusion because the heart cannot pump enough.
glossary.LAD: Left anterior descending artery; supplies the front of the heart and the septum.
glossary.thrombolysis: Clot-dissolving drugs such as alteplase; used only in STEMI when PCI is not timely.
glossary.morphine: Opioid painkiller used for ongoing ischaemic chest pain.
glossary.hs-Troponin: High-sensitivity troponin assay, repeated after a few hours to look for a rise.
